p:
Thank you so much, Commissioner, for your testimony. I want to recognize that we've been joined by our Finance Chair and Committee Member,

Council Member Linda Lee, and also Council Member Sandra Ung. First, before getting started, Commissioner, I want to thank you for all your service to our City, the work that you've done. I've been aware of your work over these years, too, even as the First Deputy Commissioner as well, and now as the Acting Commissioner of this agency, too. It's very much appreciated. These are very turbulent times, and DOI played a leading role in ensuring that the City rooted out corruption and moved forward. And on a personal note, you knew me 20 years ago when I was a first-year law school intern in the Manhattan DA's office, so it's been an honor to at least, for the last couple hearings, be in this role together years later. It comes full circle. So thank you for all your service to the City, and best wishes on your next endeavor as well.
Thank you.

I want to get started by, you give a lot of information here, you know, just about the state of the budget and where we are right now, but I want to zoom out for a minute and just highlight a few key things that you

mentioned. In Fiscal Year 2025, the Department received 14,435 complaints, which led to 1,515 active investigations and 782 referrals for civil and administrative action and criminal prosecution. Does those numbers sound correct to you in terms of the work and scale of complaints and investigations you all did?
Yes.

And you also mentioned, I think in the beginning of your testimony too, the amount of work that DOI had done on criminal cases, from the indictment of former Mayor Adams' Chief Advisor and eight other co-defendants, 70 employees at NYCHA, ACS, FDNY, various levels of fraud, and other landlords that were indicted for harassing rent-regulated tenants, just to name a few. Is that a correct summary of all the work that you had done?
It was a sampling of the work we have done. It goes obviously well beyond that, but those are matters that we thought we would highlight.

And in this year's preliminary budget, the current proposal is, despite

all of that work, 54 million in this preliminary budget, right?
Correct.
And as you mentioned, that is, going back for the last five years, a 4-million-dollar decline in the budget, if I had that right, in the preliminary budget for DOI as well. Is that right?
Correct.
And about five years ago, you all had a staff of 525, and now you all have a staff of 417, which, as you mentioned, 108 fewer staff doing oversight over the last five years. Is that right?
Correct.

And that is despite the fact that expenses and salaries have risen, and even more so despite the fact that the City budget workforce has remained stable, and in fact the budget has gone up from 95 billion to 127 billion. Is that right?
Correct.

So, budget's gone up, workforce has remained stable, yet during that

time, DOI's resources and budget have drastically been reduced. Is that right?
Correct.

And that is also during a time where you all were not only doing a number of different investigations and complaints, but where you all were investigating and bringing forward and recommending for charges criminal activity occurring at the highest levels of City Hall. Is that correct?
Correct.
Which ultimately led to a change in leadership at City Hall as well, and a number of federal and state indictments that came out as a result of that work too from DOI. Is that right?
Yes.

So that is really what stuns me today. Commissioner, do you believe that an agency with a mission as important as the Department of Investigation to root out corruption at every level of government, do you believe that the budget of an agency like that should be subject to the whims of City Hall, to the whims and the results

of investigations that you all undertake? Do you believe that that should have any bearing on the budget you all receive as DOI?

No. I believe it was last year DOI worked with and certainly made a proposal in the Charter revision process to come up with a way to prevent exactly what you're describing. And what we proposed was pegging DOI's budget as a percentage of the City budget to remove even the appearance that an administration would be intentionally defunding the oversight agency. And so if DOI's budget was pegged in a particular way, and I think we recommended a percentage of the City budget at 0.06 percent, if the budget rose, so would DOI's budget. If the budget was reduced, so would ours. But it would remove any ability or even the appearance that our budget was being manipulated for in order to reduce the ability of the agency to conduct oversight. We had made that proposal. It is a sound methodology that is used by other cities. And we talked to some of our colleagues in other cities who operated under that same regimen, and so we made that recommendation last year.
So, you all proposed, as part of the Charter Revision Commission, funding and basing the funding of the important agency, and this agency's important work, based on a percentage of the City budget.
Correct.
And that was done to protect the independence of the Department of Investigations, right?
Correct.

And that independence is a critical element of DOI's work because you are examining, investigating corruption at every level of City government, from any City employee to the top of city hall. Is that correct?
Yes.
What happened to that proposal that you all had put forward?

Yeah. So, it's our understanding that our proposal is within one of the two kind of competing Charter revision sets of proposals that stand now. Whether or not ours will be adopted, I don't think we know that.
So a proposal as important as this has been, so to speak, lost in the sauce of the dueling Charter Revision Commissions, one put forth by former Mayor Adams. Is that right?
Correct.

You know, what really stuns me about this is given the importance of DOI's mission and mandate, given the crucial role that DOI played in the investigation and federal charges that ultimately led to the indictment of former Mayor Adams, given the importance of DOI's independence to do that work, to see the budget slashed over these years, to see the staffing slashed over these years is just shocking. And it raises serious questions, in my mind, about the hollowing out of this agency by a prior Administration that themselves were the subject of sprawling Federal and State investigations that DOI was a part of. I don't believe any agency should be subject to the whims of politics that way, but an agency with such an important independent mandate like DOI's, to see it subjected to political games the way that it has been the last four years is frankly part of the problem and part of what we need to address moving forward

with this new Administration and with this new era in City government. My question is, to the extent you can reveal, what were the conversations like with the Department of Investigations and the prior Administration when it came to funding for DOI, whether it's with OMB or the Mayor's Office? How did those conversations go when it came to hiring, budget modifications, or interagency coordination? I'm sure you all, I was there for your testimony, for prior budget hearings. To the extent you can disclose, what were the outcomes of those discussions with City Hall? Where did they go? We know what happened in the budget itself and the resources you got and didn't get, but was DOI making its case to City Hall as to the importance of these resources?

Unquestionably, DOI was repeatedly, at every opportunity, making its case with the prior Administration, particularly through OMB and through City Hall. All the proposals, everything that was included in my testimony today, the facts, the figures, the downward trend, we made our case at every opportunity that we had with the last Administration.
And what was the reaction that you received?

We had some positive responses on particularized requests, but generally speaking, the largest ticket items that we had requested that would really have the most significant structural impact on the agency, in terms of hiring and salary and retention, were not acted on by the Administration. And we were repeatedly subject to PEGs and reductions and the cost cutting that puts us in the position we are in now.

Which is shocking to me, because we have not seen, since the days of Tammany Hall, the level of corruption we saw at City Hall over the last four years. And you all are tasked with investigating and rooting out that corruption, which you did very commendably. Do you all feel that when the budgets get cut this way, when you see such a reduction in staffing and a 4-million-dollar decline in your budget over the last four years, does that hamper your ability to conduct the anti-corruption and other investigations that you all do at the Department of Investigation?

As I said in my testimony, it certainly has negatively impacted our ability to do everything that we want to do. I will say that the staff at DOI is committed to this mission and there are things that we would want to do, but that they are reduced in our ability to do so. However, we continue to do day-to-day the important work and make do with what we can. So, the mission is there. The staff is dedicated to the work. It would be disingenuous to say that it has not impacted our day-to-day ability to do the work. It simply causes us to triage more and to decide where can we dedicate the scarce resources that we have to deliver the most meaningful impact for the City. So, it certainly is a balancing act and a prioritization, which I think we've been very effective in doing. We certainly needed to do the large-scale, labor-intensive, high-profile cases last year. I think the City needed us to do that. And while keeping the day-to-day work going, it was asking a lot of staff. Staff were asked to do a lot more with a lot less and a lot fewer of them. So, it has been a challenge, but the staff is admirably dedicated to the work that we do.

Which, as you pointed out at the end, and that's the key, you all have done a lot more with a lot less. And very commendably, so may I add. But it is very surprising to see that this preliminary budget only proposes 54 million dollars for an agency with such a broad and critical mandate across the city. I have a few more questions, and I'm going to turn it over to our Finance Chair to ask some questions as well. So, my first question is, since the start of the Adams Administration, the Department's budgeted head count has been reduced by 28 percent, and we know the impact that that has, and you testified to it as well. Can you point to a time when you felt the Department's funding was at an optimal level?

I don't think we can necessarily point to a particular point in time. But when the opportunity to rethink our budget, and we did this under Commissioner Strauber's leadership last year, we did a really deep dive, deliberate assessment, because we knew we would be asking, in the Charter revision context, for

something durable, ad so we took an extraordinary deep dive and really analyzed unit by unit within DOI what we would need without asking. We remember this is still government so, we were not asking for anything that we thought was extravagant. But we did an analysis, unit by unit, of what we would need to really optimize the performance of our squad. And that is where we came to that pegging of the budget idea at .066 percent. That would be, in our collective assessment, an optimal point. I believe it would bring our budget into the something like 72 million or so and bring our headcount into the high sixes or the low sevens, inclusive of on loans from other agencies. But that would be a really optimal situation without it being asking more than we would credibly be able to ask.
Right. And how many cities, or can you name a few of them, have adopted this model of tying their DOI budgets to the city budget?

We spent a lot of time speaking with our colleagues in Chicago who have been operating under this regimen for a very long time. It is also an extraordinarily productive

and insightful office that has been very generous with their time. And we talk to each other in the inspector general world. But the one that comes to mind was Chicago. They've operated under this. And they were very helpful in walking us through thinking how to pick the right number. Obviously, it's a Charter revision, so we wanted to get this right. And I think we believe we got a reasonable, proper number. And I'm sure we may have spoken with Los Angeles as well, but I actually don't remember that right now.
Got it. And you mentioned before, that would bring the overall headcount to high 600s, low 700s, right?
Yes.

Should be an optimal amount. Commissioner Strauber mentioned at a prior budget hearing, the Department couldn't perform proactive investigations due to headcount restrictions. Is that still the case? And is this optimal budget that you've testified to, what you need to proactively stop fraud and waste? I mean, I

think it's clear to everybody that we've got to make sure we stop bad actors and bad behavior before it actually happens. So, what is the status of these proactive investigations?

So, what I think the point Commissioner Strauber was making is that we have to balance our proactive work and our complaint-driven work, the 13,000, 14,000 complaints that come in every year. DOI looks at them. We look at everyone and make some determination whether it's something that we can refer to another City agency, whether it's something that really falls within the purview of DOI. But we do that work, obviously, every day. We are engaged in proactive investigations all the time, and so it's not necessarily an either-or, but it is a balancing act. I believe that is what Commissioner Strauber was describing when she testified. And it goes back to, I think, my prior comments. There is a triaging of opportunities. DOI has all sorts of opportunities to do lots of very productive, impactful work. We want our work to be as impactful as possible. And if it's a matter of doing a proactive investigation, we want to do the most impactful ones that help agencies perform better,

services to be delivered more effectively by the city, and have, again, also the psychological impact, both for City employees, that DOI is here. Our numbers are down, but we are still here and we are still actively working with agencies on issues of corruption but also to let the public know that DOI is still actively doing our job. Every City agency is operating under constraints, but we want to pick the proactive work that is the most impactful. And I think we've been able to do that.

And just a couple more questions from my side, at least for a bit. You testified about the asset forfeiture funding that you all use, which, to me, what was very shocking about that for prior budget hearings is how much you all rely on asset forfeiture funds to fund important needs of the Department. And as you mentioned before, federal guidelines also emphasize that asset forfeiture funds cannot supplant any core funding from the City and for operations. They can only supplement. But it seems to me that you all have been using it for any new needs that come up. And in particular, from one case where, over time, obviously, those funds will diminish. So, I just want

to get a better sense of how much funding has the Department had to utilize from the asset forfeiture funds over the years? And how much baseline OTPS funding does the Department need added in the next fiscal year so you don't have to utilize asset forfeiture funds?

Give me one moment. So going back, I'll just give you a sampling of some years. Going back to Fiscal Year '23, our forfeiture spend, and it's a combination of Department of Justice, Department of Treasury, and State forfeiture. Our forfeiture spend in Fiscal Year '23 was 1.37 million. In '24, that rose to 3.62 million. In Fiscal Year '25, our expenditure was 6.97 million. In '26, our current obligations for which we have dedicated forfeiture is 7.3 million. And we believe our forecast would be that should rise to 9.9 million, or another 2.6 million additionally in 2026, in order to fund our operations. So, to your question, what we would need from City tax levy to fill that gap, essentially, those are the numbers.

So, Commissioner, can I just pause on that for a minute? So, from FY23, 1.37 million drawn from forfeiture. And then FY26, currently 7.3 million, but likely ending up at about 9.9 million by the end. So, 1.3 to 9.9. So, 8.6-million-dollar increase over the last several years in drawing down on the asset forfeiture funds. Is that right?
Correct.
And that's obviously results of the budget declining, and you all needing to pull that money from somewhere to be able to, is it to sustain operations, or is it for new needs as well?

I can check with my colleagues, I would categorize it as sustaining operations in the sense, I mean, I'll give you just one example. Our case management system. DOI had an antiquated case management system, which was not able to function properly or adequately for the internal needs. With the changes in discovery law that we saw over the last few years, and I think other agencies have dealt with as well, we needed a system that would allow us to be able to manage

internal data in a way that would allow us to be more productive internally, but also to be able to comply with state, the compliance of discovery. And so we use forfeiture for that. It's both a new need, but I would consider that, you know, kind of more of an internal maintenance. We're not looking for something in addition to what we had. We were replacing something that was old and not working with something that was new and modern and more effective for our internal needs. But it wasn't, you know, it was an internal maintenance need.
It was new needs, but to sustain core operations.
Correct, yes.

Right. Have other cities, Department of Investigations, I mean, you all are talking to their IG offices, even law enforcement agencies. Have you seen that much reliance on asset forfeiture funds to fund that level of, you know, new needs, but to sustain core operations?

I don't know specifically the answer to that. It's something we would certainly be able to find out and get back to

the Committee on. My suspicion is, I mean, New York is unique, and the reason why we have the forfeiture funds we have would largely emanate from the CityTime case, which was a long time ago, but only released within, you know, several years ago. But for that particular case, we would not have the forfeiture that we have. So, it's possible that other cities have similar forfeiture experiences, but like, unless there is a case like that. So, I would largely think the answer would be no, but I could certainly confirm that and get back to the Council.

And my final question is just, you know, you mentioned the CityTime case. That was where a lot of the asset forfeiture funds are coming from. How much is left in that fund? And at the rate you all are drawing down, when would that fund be depleted?
So, at our current rate of spend, we would deplete that reserve in two to four years.
Two to four years?
Correct, yeah.
And how much is left in that fund?

The DOI received 32 million from that, and there's 20 million left. So, we received that in 2022, that 32 million that is now in the current year 20 million. But as you can see by the rate of spend, it's simply not sustainable.

And lastly, if you all did tie your agency's budget to the City budget, or saw an increase in the agency budget in other ways, you would not need to draw down at that asset forfeiture fund at that rate, right?

Correct, not at that rate. I mean, forfeiture funds need to be spent. They can't be squirreled away. And so, there's an obligation to spend them, but this is unusual. So, yes, if we were to receive the adequate funding, that rate of spend would change dramatically.
Thank you. I'm going to turn it over now to our Finance Chair to ask questions.
Hi. Good afternoon.
Good afternoon.

So, a really quick question on just the Chief Savings Officers, because

I know every agency is being asked to do this. So, have you identified someone actually within the agency to be the Chief Savings Officer?

We have. We have a wonderful Chief Savings Officer. She is here today. Deputy Commissioner Kaytlin Simmons is our head of all things, operations and heads up finance, and she is our Chief Savings Officer.
Awesome. Nice to meet you. I think the target reductions for FY26 and '27 are the same, I'm assuming, right, which is 1.5 percent for FY26, and then 2.5 percent for FY27?
Yes. That's correct.

Okay. And have you identified, I know the reports are technically due Friday, but have you identified any areas in where savings can be found, and has the administration looked to decrease or eliminate any units for savings?

One moment. So, yes, DOI has been asked to find 1.5 percent in savings in 2026 and 2.5 percent in Fiscal Year '27

and the outyears. We have been struggling to identify areas for cuts. Again, as I said in my testimony, we are not a programmatic agency. We are people, equipment, that's really what we have to cut. We're already very lean. We don't have excessive spending. Any cuts will impact DOI's ability to fulfill its mission. There's no getting around that. We will do everything we can to, you know, effectively perform our mission as best as possible, but any cuts will reduce our ability to do that and to determine where best to focus our remaining resources. We will continue that triaging of resources. Our three primary drivers of our budget are salaries, rent, and the two integrity monitorships, none of which we have the ability to cut if we wanted to.
Right. Well, that's my follow-up question. So, are you subject to the vacancy reductions and are there any positions that are exempt?
We are subject to the vacancy reduction, and the answer to exemption is no.
Okay. Perfect. Thank you so much.
Thank you.

Thank you, Chair. Council Member Ung, do you have any questions? Going back to a few different areas to look at. Well, my first question is, oh, sorry, going back to the asset forfeiture. You mentioned that there are statutory requirements to draw down over the funds over time. They can't just sit there. So, what are the statutory timelines for that? I mean, when are you required or legally obligated to draw down at what rate? How does that work?

My understanding is there is no predetermined rate of spend that is required by DOJ, Treasury, or the State. They're there to help agencies, you know, supplement budgets. So, we would want to use forfeiture to enhance the services that we deliver to the City to work more proactively with agencies. There's a lot we can do with forfeiture. So, we would certainly be spending them. But there is no particular duration by which they have to be spent or any rate of spend that's required, but we would

certainly want to use them to enhance our oversight of City agencies.
And going back to the reports that you all issue, how many mandated and unmandated reports has the Department issued in the last year? How does that compare to previous years?

One moment. I have that right here. So, in 2025, DOI issued 14 reports. Two of those were mandated. Just to give you some kind of a comparison, in 2024, we did 15 reports, five were mandated. In 2023, we did nine, and three were mandated. And in 2022, we did four. So we're averaging, in recent years, about 14, 15 reports a year.
But presumably with less staff and less resources, that's more burdensome on the existing staff to keep up that pace.

It's harder to do. We have staff who are the subject matter experts who are finding themselves in the field more to try to get them now to come in, sit and actually write an investigative report. It's doable. We're doing it. We will continue to do it. And we are moving resources

around in order to make sure that we fulfill that obligation to the City. But absolutely correct. It is increasingly difficult to do. And I think our reports tend to be really, really impactful and really meaningful and are designed to speak not only to policymakers but to the public to let them know how their City agencies that provide services to them are performing, and we note ways that DOI improves City services. I think it's very important for the public to see that. Again, we'll keep doing it. It's going to become increasingly harder to do at that rate.
And to the extent you can disclose, what reports are you working on now?

So, what I can share publicly is the Office of the Inspector General for the NYPD is currently working on its annual report. And we are also working on the POST act report, which this year will be focusing on the NYPD's use of facial recognition technology, which is, I think, something that's widely of interest to individuals in the public and policymakers. We're also working on our annual anti-corruption report, which will look at the auditing capabilities of City

agencies. And we're also working on a report that will detail the challenges that we have in exercising independent oversight of ACS because of certain State laws that restrict our ability to access their records, as well as the restrictive manner in which the State's Office of Children and Family Services exercises its limited discretionary authority to approve our access to records. Finally, our Protest Response Oversight Unit is working on the first of their reports that they will be releasing this spring.

Thank you. And I want to go through a couple of different areas that you testified to before about the work you're all doing and how the budget impacts that. So, you mentioned or, you know, we've heard a bit about the Vendor Integrity Unit that DOI has that oversees the monitor program, DEP projects and vendor name checks for contracts over 250,000. What is the budget and headcount for this unit? Is it fully staffed?

So, yes. So, one moment. So, the current headcount of Vendor

Integrity is 18. It's split between three areas. One is the inspector general for Vendor Integrity who has three staff members here in the City, and the inspector general manages all of the City's monitorships, of which I believe there are probably about 10 operating right now. Those include some of the big-ticket items like the Borough-based jail monitorship, which we are engaged in currently. The asylum seeker monitorship from the last couple of years, which was obviously a wide-ranging enterprise. We also have the Vendex unit, which runs name checks on City vendors. We also have, which is probably lesser known, we have seven staff members in, I'll call it upstate New York because I'm from Queens, so everything is upstate, but they're up in near Poughkeepsie and they operate the watershed. So, we have investigators, largely capital construction funded by DEP, but we have an entire staff up there doing operational work to protect the watershed and the New York City drinking water, which is something that's interesting. They are largely fully staffed. We have a couple openings, but I think we're in the process of onboarding at least one or two. So, we're very close to being fully staffed.

And could this unit investigate and provide oversight into the varying contract costs that agencies have for similar services? What will the unit need to perform its duty or do you feel like it's sufficiently back to this point?

It would be very difficult for this unit to perform that function. During the pendency of the asylum seeker monitorship, we worked, this unit worked very closely with the assigned monitor in real-time monitoring of contracts across City agencies and actually did, I think, a remarkable job of communicating contract costs, per unit costs that were by contract, by agency. So, the agencies could see, we're spending more for this and you're spending less for this to be able to look at their contract costs. To do that on our own, we did that with KPMG as an exterior, as an outside monitor. For DOI to replicate that, we certainly could. It would require funding for the appropriate personnel with the appropriate training.

And you testified to this a bit before too, but for the 9/11

investigation mandate, what are the budget requests for that?
The final budget request will be 4 to 5 million.

And for NYPD OIG, the preliminary plan includes 1.7 million and 17 positions in FY27. Is this sufficient funding to provide oversight to the NYPD? What are the challenges in hiring and retaining an inspector general for this position?

So, we think the funding is appropriate. We've got to a staffing level. We had the opportunity to hire up new staff, as I said earlier, sometime mid last year. We have a terrific staff. They are well underway in their work. So, I think their current staffing, given the systemic work that they're doing, is appropriate. In terms of identifying and onboarding an inspector general, we've certainly been exploring that. It's something we very much wanted to do with the new Commissioner.

And when it comes to housing investigations, I've got a particular interest in them too, as a former tenant's lawyer,

and looking at the ways in which DOI can play a role in ensuring that tenants have robust protections and that landlords are held accountable, as you all are doing. The Administration recently announced a 2.1-million-dollar settlement with a landlord who was responsible for terrible housing conditions. And this, I would think, would signal a larger push by the Administration to hold landlords accountable. What is the staffing for Squads number three and number seven? I know these are the squads that oversee DOB and HPD. That's Squad three, and Squad seven oversees NYCHA. So, what is their current staffing?
So, squad three, which oversees HPD buildings, has a staff of 16. Squad seven, which oversees NYCHA, has a staff of 51.
And how does Squad three play a role in investigating hazardous conditions and tenant harassment for City-funded projects?

So, the IG for Squad three is a subject matter expert who has longstanding relationships within both the Department

of Buildings and Housing Preservation and Development. He's really knowledgeable about this area and very innovative in thinking about ways to use limited staff to have the most impact. And I won't say it's new, but I think it's probably the best in a long time. Our relationship with the DA's offices, both the IG and the executive staff, we're constantly in contact with our partners at the five DA's offices, talking about these issues and looking for opportunities to work together. Everything we do in the tenant harassment field, we share very early and often both ways with the DA's offices. It's a very cooperative and collaborative relationship that has really both brought really effective cases, but brought cases quicker. Anytime you have an allegation that a tenant is being harassed, time is of the essence. Unlike other investigations where you might give more time, that's something we want to act on very, very quickly. And the DA's have been great. That Squad also responds to building collapses, fires, along with DOB staff. We see on New York One something happening that fire and DOB are out at, DOI has staff members responding as well.
And are any squads in desperate need of additional staff or resources?

I don't know how we define desperate. Every squad has significantly fewer individuals than it did at three or four or five years ago. We need more staff. We are a people agency, as I've said two or three times already. We are run by people. We are lean. We don't have extravagant spending on anything beyond people, vehicles, computers, and rent. Those are the things that we need. If we have more people, DOI can continue to do the job that the City expects it to do.
And, of course, you're also moving around inspectors between squads too, right, as needs arise?
We are --
Investigators, sorry.
We're certainly moving staff depending on the needs of any project. It's all hands-on deck all the time.

And when it comes to the Protest Settlement Monitor Unit, the Council

had pushed for in the last budget approximately 600,000 to be included to create that unit with five staff. Have you hired for all these positions? And do you feel that five positions are enough to conduct the oversight that this unit is responsible for doing?

Yes. We've hired one inspector general, two investigative attorneys, I believe that's their title, and two investigators. They are a remarkably experienced, highly skilled group. They've done a tremendous job to date. And I think they are adequately funded and staffed.
And how is the staffing for Squad one that oversees the Department of Probations?
Squad one's total staffing stands at 24, and that's a combination of DOI staff and on loan staff from

Got it. Okay. And recently the Department referred over a case investigating the former Commissioner. Can you talk a bit with public detail about that was a referral that was made from you all over to City

authorities, I believe, to the DA's office, or I may be misremembering that, or maybe not. But if you can, to the extent you can, publicly disclose the substance of that referral and who it was made to.
I can't.
Are there other pending cases the Department is looking into? Are there other pending cases the Department is looking into? Concerning the Department of Probation? Also, if you can.
Also, not something I can talk about.
To the extent you can disclose this, will there be a report on the findings that you all, from your investigations?

Whenever we do an investigation, depending on what the outcome is, one of the options is to do a report, yes. What the outcome for anything relating to the Department of Probation, it would be too early to know what the ultimate outcome would be.

Got it. Thank you. And according to the FY25 Mayor's Management Report, the average time to complete

investigation took 251 days, which is 20 percent increase from the four-year average between 2021 and 2024 of 208 days so, it's gone up by about 43 days. The Department target for this indicator is 180 days. Could you tell us a little bit more about what may be causing this increase?

I think everything that we have talked about today is responsible for the source of that continued up. Certainly, there is manpower, certainly, there's resources. I think also when you have, you know, 180 is the goal. Not all cases fall within that being a reasonable expectation, particularly long-term investigations of high-ranking officials in City government. Those tend to skew the timeframe. So, I would suspect that that is also the investigations that have been public over the last year and a half or two are very much not something that the 180-day kind of is even a reasonable thought.

Sure. Well, those are all the questions we had, Commissioner. You know, I think one of the big themes we see today is we appreciate all that DOI has done

so much and more that DOI has done with far less. But as we stated and began this hearing by commenting on, I do strongly believe that you all deserve and need the resources commensurate with the critical work that you're all doing when it comes to transparency and accountability in government so we'll keep pushing for that on our end. And I think it's critical to see the differences in this new budget as well, given what's transpired over the last four years. But I want to thank you all for your work. Thank the staff of DOI as well and appreciate your leadership too.

Testimony before the City Council Committee on Oversight and Investigations City Hall – March 18, 2026

Preliminary Budget for Fiscal Year 2027

Good afternoon, members of the New York City Council Committee on Oversight and Investigations. My name is Ben Weinberg, and I am the Director of Public Policy at Citizens Union. Citizens Union is a nonpartisan good government group working to ensure honest and accountable government, fair and open elections, and a civically engaged public. We congratulate Council Member Shekar Krishnan on his appointment as chair of this important committee and appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the preliminary budget for Fiscal Year 2027. We urge the Council to provide increased funding in the FY2027 budget for the city’s ethics and anticorruption watchdogs beyond the levels proposed in the mayor’s preliminary budget. This includes both the Department of Investigation (DOI), which is the subject of today’s hearing, and the Conflicts of Interest Board (COIB), which does not receive a dedicated budget oversight hearing. Both DOI and COIB experienced budget reductions, funding freezes, and significant attrition under the previous administration. Yet Mayor Mamadni’s preliminary budget keeps their funding largely flat compared with the most recent financial plan. The need to ensure a clean and ethical government, however, has not remained flat. If anything, it has grown in the wake of the ethical misconduct that marked the previous administration. As the size and complexity of city government— and its budget— continue to increase, so too must the capacity of the agencies responsible for safeguarding its integrity. Recent years have demonstrated why these agencies must be adequately resourced to function as truly independent watchdogs. As DOI and COIB pursued matters involving City Hall officials, they were affected by Office of Management and Budget refusals to authorize the filling of vacancies. The former DOI commissioner suggested that requests for support received limited response as investigations involving City Hall became public. 1 A charter commission appointed by the City Council last year recognized these challenges and the need to strengthen the capacity of both agencies, including addressing chronic staffing reductions and
1 Greg Smith, THE CITY, 01/22/2026. Adams Hired Her. She Probed Him. Mamdani Let Her Leave https://www.thecity.nyc/2026/01/22/jocelyn-strauber-doi-department-investigation-exit-interview-eric-adams/

ensuring sufficient funding for non-salary expenses. The Commission to Strengthen Local Democracy recommended in its final report that the budgets of DOI and COIB be increased and protected, setting minimum funding levels of 0.06 percent and 0.0035 percent of the city’s total budget, respectively. The agencies’ FY2027 budget requests are more modest than those recommended levels, and we urge the Council to include them in its budget response. We support DOI’s request for 17 new full-time positions to assist with investigations, background checks, and operations. These additions would bring DOI to a total of 326 full-time employees— still significantly below the 408 positions in FY 2020. DOI also requires additional OTPS funding to keep pace with technological developments. In addition, a recent Council resolution directing DOI to investigate what the city knew about Ground Zero toxins following the September 11 attacks will likely require further resources (Reso. 560-2024). At the same time, DOI’s workload has increased significantly. The number of complaints received, arrests made, and cases referred for prosecution has risen in recent years, even as staffing levels have declined. This strain is reflected in the Fiscal 2026 Preliminary Mayor’s Management Report metrics: the time required to complete investigations increased from an average of 201 days in FY2023 to 251 days in FY2025, and to 325 days in the first four months of FY2026; the average time to complete a background investigation increased to 117 days in the first four months of this fiscal year, compared to 109-day average during the first four months of FY2025. We also support restoring COIB’s staffing levels. In January 2022, COIB had a staff of 26; today it has only 20, with approval to fill two vacancies that would bring the total to 22. The mayor’s proposed budget keeps funding flat at $2.86 million, effectively returning COIB to the same budget level it had prior to the Adams administration, despite substantial growth in the city’s overall budget and the effects of inflation. The widening gap between the scale of city government and the small agency responsible for enforcing its ethics laws poses a real risk to maintaining a clean and honest government. COIB should receive sufficient funding to restore its staffing to 26 positions. This would allow the Board to better support the city workforce by strengthening its advice, education, and legal units. Adequate funding is also necessary to retain experienced staff. In an agency of COIB’s size, retention is critical to preserving institutional knowledge and maintaining operational integrity. Looking ahead, we also strongly support establishing charter-protected minimum funding levels for both DOI and COIB to help ensure their independence and stability over time. We urge the Council to continue advancing the reforms proposed by its own Charter Revision Commission. These thoughtful measures should be placed on the ballot, either by the Commission to Strengthen Local Democracy or as part of any future mayoral Charter Revision Commission. Investing in oversight agencies is an investment in a more efficient and effective city government. DOI investigations alone resulted in more than $6 million in financial recoveries last year and helped generate millions more in savings through oversight of contracts, vendors, and procurement processes. COIB trains tens of thousands of city employees each year, helping ensure that those entrusted with public resources do not misuse their authority. For these reasons, we urge the City Council to ensure that DOI and COIB receive the resources necessary to effectively carry out their critical oversight responsibilities.

Frank Morano
